analysis.title: Nothing Good Happens Below The 200-Day Moving Average...
key_insights: The S&P 500 fell back below its 200-day moving average (7,348) on Nov 19 after an early squeeze attempt failed. It was on track for a sixth straight daily decline, the longest losing streak since April 2024, with all 11 sectors red.

BTIG's Krinsky screened 30 years for six-day losing streaks that close below the 200DMA by no more than 3%. There were three: 9/27/00, 10/11/18 and 2/27/20. All three saw the SPX higher five days later, then meaningful downside.

After the five-day bounces (2.5%, 3.9%, 5.4%), the three prior episodes fell 26% (2000), 16.7% (2018) and 30% (2020). The article's illustrative average bounce is about 3.9% (to roughly 7,530) and the average drawdown about 24%. It notes the sample of three makes this illustrative only.

Krinsky's SPX target remains 7,000-7,100. The intraday low was 7,193. He expects a move closer to 7k because there has been no sustained correlation-one capitulation (74% downside volume at about 1:00pm, AAPL down less than 1%).
Krinsky would use any pre-Thanksgiving bounce to fade it, anticipating another leg lower. Goldman's Privorotsky argued that holding the 200d into Thanksgiving could let 'stability beget stability'.

Privorotsky's squeeze case rested on an 11-point hedge fund underweight in tech (roughly the deepest in five years, per Goldman Prime), dealers 'very short' gamma and a friendly holiday calendar. Short gamma amplifies moves in both directions, and the move went down.

Anthropic's IPO opened 34% above its $83 offer with a $107 billion allocation, 60% of which was unfilled. Chip stocks erased early gains after the first print, and the article says funds sold other holdings to make room.

BTIG's XLV (healthcare) is down 5.7% over four days, its largest such move since April 2025. Krinsky sees further downside toward 175 from about $178. Per Bloomberg, health care and consumer staples led the decline across sectors.

BTIG is easing its bearish gold stance. Gold futures are at $3,685 against a roughly $3,500/oz downside target, and Krinsky says sentiment is washed out and conditions oversold. He says this is not a reversal to a constructive stance ('Sometimes there is no fat pitch').
Privorotsky says a strong dollar, high real rates and credit yields compete with gold. Goldman's commodity team still expects central bank buying to support gold.

The article's author sides with Krinsky on the medium-term direction. Reasons given: the Fed minutes say 'almost all' members want to hike more, disinflation is coming from falling commodities, weaker capex and Australian job losses, and there is an AI debt pile. A Fed change is needed to reverse the market.

market_movers.rationale: BTIG has been negative on large-cap healthcare since it reached a 19% premium to its 200DMA. XLV is down 5.7% in four days and BTIG sees more downside toward 175.

BTIG notes AAPL was down less than 1% on a day the SPX fell sharply, which it reads as no capitulation yet. A prior back-to-back exhaustion signal in AAPL preceded negative 20-day returns 89% of the time.

sector_views.rationale: BTIG has been negative on XLV since it stretched to a 19% premium over its 200DMA. It sees downside toward 175 before risk/reward turns neutral.
Goldman Prime data show hedge funds running an 11-point underweight in tech, which Privorotsky sees as squeeze fuel. Chip stocks erased their gains after the Anthropic IPO opened.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The SPX at about 7,249 was roughly 100 points below the 200DMA. It first closed below it on Tuesday, for the first time since April.
A 7,000 level would be about 10.8% below the October record of 7,844.62, which is correction territory.
Gold fell below $3,800 on Wednesday alongside crypto as the dollar and bonds caught a bid. BTIG's downside target is about $3,500/oz.
Elevated volatility alongside short dealer gamma, which amplifies moves in both directions.

risk_factors: Sixth straight SPX decline with the index below its 200DMA. The three historical analogues all saw large drawdowns after a short bounce.
Short dealer gamma amplifies moves in both directions.
Defensive sectors (healthcare, staples) are now falling, which suggests funds are selling whatever has a gain.
Fed minutes show 'almost all' members want to hike more.
Disinflation is coming from falling commodities, fading capex and Australian job losses.
A debt pile tied to AI and a record IPO that drew liquidity from other assets.
